sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914 and shelled Belgrade the same day. Its officers expected a short punitive campaign that would free troops for the war against Russia.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Serbia's plan was to stay on the defensive until the direction of the main invasion became clear, and to draw in as many Austro-Hungarian troops as possible to weaken the effort against Russia.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Oskar Potiorek, governor of Bosnia and Herzegovina, commanded the invasion. His Fifth Army crossed the Drina to break into north-west Serbia, while the Second Army on the Sava threatened Šabac and Belgrade. The Serbian Supreme Command under Radomir Putnik had expected the main attack from the north and had to shift its forces west.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Cer is a mountain ridge in north-west Serbia between the Jadar valley and the plain of Mačva, with Šabac to the north-east and Loznica on the Drina to the west. The Austro-Hungarian corps advanced along both the ridge and the Jadar valley.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Putnik's Supreme Command directed three armies: the First under Petar Bojović, the Second under Stepa Stepanović and the Third under Pavle Jurišić Šturm. On the Austro-Hungarian side the Fifth Army's 8th and 13th Corps led the invasion, with the Sixth Army in Bosnia and the Second Army on the Sava. The Second Army was redirected toward Galicia on 18 August, so the invasion went ahead with fewer troops than planned. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Austro-Hungarian attack began on the morning of 12 August, and after two days the corps were across the Drina, pressing the Serbian Third Army's outposts. Šabac was bombarded and taken. Stepanović's Second Army was ordered west to support the Third, sending its Combined Division and 1st Morava Division toward Cer.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On the night of 15–16 August a regiment of the Combined Division met the Austro-Hungarian 21st Division near Tekeriš and drove it back toward the Drina. The next day the 9th Division struck the Combined Division's flank and forced it back, until the 1st Morava Division arrived and Stepanović himself came to the front line. Meanwhile the Third Army was pushed back up the Jadar valley. On 17 and 18 August both sides attacked along the ridge; the 2nd Morava Division restored the Third Army's position. Under constant attack, the 9th Division gave way, exposing the 13th Corps in the Jadar valley, and on the night of 19–20 August the Fifth Army withdrew across the Drina. Šabac was retaken on 24 August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Putnik and Stepanović committed the Second Army against the flank of the invasion on Cer instead of holding a line farther east. Its cavalry cut the Šabac–Lešnica railway, and the 1st Šumadija Division was sent to Šabac to cover the troops on Cer and keep Austro-Hungarian support from reaching the Fifth Army.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The arrival of the 1st Morava Division and Stepanović's presence on 16 August stopped the crisis on the ridge; the retreat of the 9th Division on 19 August left the 13th Corps in the Jadar valley exposed and forced the whole Fifth Army back.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The invasion was thrown back across the Drina. Britannica and Tasić call Cer the first Allied victory of the war; the Serbian Ministry of Defence counts it among the Serbian army's greatest victories, won under Stepanović's command.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: During the invasion Austro-Hungarian troops killed civilians in Šabac and across Mačva and the Jadar. R. A. Reiss, a University of Lausanne professor commissioned by the Serbian government, investigated in the autumn of 1914: he documented killings of old people and children, burned villages, hostage-taking and sexual violence, and concluded that some acts were ordered or encouraged by officers. Tasić notes that the violence took place against a background of anti-Serbian propaganda and fear of Serbian irregulars, who looked no different from civilians. The victory raised Serbia's standing with its allies and ended Austro-Hungarian hopes of an easy campaign.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defender who waits for the direction of the main attack and then strikes its flank with a concentrated army can defeat an invader who has split his forces between fronts and valleys.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The battle is dated 15–20 August by Britannica, 16–20 August by Bjelajac and 17–19 August by Tasić; the fighting for Šabac ran to 24 August. Reiss's report, written at the Serbian government's request and published in wartime, records the Austro-Hungarian explanations of shots fired from houses and irregulars among civilians alongside his own findings; its figures, which he says understate the toll, are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Historical Museum of Serbia and Military Museum catalogue gives the order of battle and the day-by-day narrative. Britannica's account of the 1914 campaign and its biography of Putnik, and the 1914-1918-online articles by Dmitar Tasić and Mile Bjelajac, place the battle in the war. Reiss's 1916 report documents the violence against civilians, and the Serbian Ministry of Defence page records the memorial at Tekeriš.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the victory on Cer, Serbia went over to the offensive. Syrmia, the Austro-Hungarian land between the Sava and the Danube, lay across the Sava from the First Army's positions around Obrenovac.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The offensive was undertaken under pressure from Serbia's allies, to relieve the Russians in Galicia. Bjelajac stresses that the Serbian army was still waiting for promised rifles, ammunition and bridging equipment when the Allies insisted on it.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The aim was to take Syrmia. The Timok Division I was to cross the Sava near Mitrovica, supported by parts of the First Army west of Belgrade.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Sava, about 410 m wide at the crossing, separated Serbia from flat Syrmian farmland. Fields of standing maize limited visibility around Šašinci.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The First Army was commanded by Petar Bojović; the Timok Division I by Vladimir Kondić. On the Austro-Hungarian side the 29th Infantry Division met the crossing. Strengths and the prisoner figures given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kondić received the order at 7 a.m. on 5 September to cross between Mitrovica and Jarak that night. His division was about 35 km from the river and tired by a night march, and its bridging material was incomplete.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The First Army crossed the Sava on the night of 5–6 September. At Šašinci the first boats of the Timok Division I crossed at 7.40 a.m. on 6 September and a pontoon bridge was begun, but Austro-Hungarian regiments counterattacked through the afternoon and evening; at night their guns fired on the bridge, which collapsed under the weight of retreating troops, and many Serbian soldiers were captured. Farther east, by 11 September the First Army's units had reached the line Nova Pazova–Vojka–Popinci–Budjanovac. The offensive was then broken off because of the Austro-Hungarian attack on the Drina, and the First Army was moved south toward Ljubovija.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Serbian Supreme Command accepted an offensive it had reason to think premature. Once the second Austro-Hungarian invasion began on the Drina, it gave priority to the defence of Serbia and pulled the First Army back.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The repulse at Šašinci on 6 September ended the attempt to take Syrmia; the Theresian Military Academy's account says it also cost the First Army its bridgehead at Kupinovo.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The offensive was aborted. The Timok Division I was not destroyed and was soon back in action after reinforcement.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The First Army reinforced the Third on the Drina, where its arrival on Mount Soko helped ease a crisis on 17 September.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A river crossing made in haste, without reconnaissance, rested and close-up troops or complete bridging equipment, is vulnerable to a prompt local counterattack; coalition pressure can push an army into operations it is not ready for.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Serbian and Austrian accounts frame the operation differently: the Serbian catalogue stresses the First Army's advance and its recall for the Drina, the Austrian academy's account the victory at Šašinci, for which Austro-Hungarian officers received the Military Order of Maria Theresa. The end date of the offensive is not given in the sources read here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Historical Museum of Serbia and Military Museum catalogue gives the Serbian narrative, and Thomas Lampersberger's article for the Theresian Military Academy the Austro-Hungarian account of Šašinci (in German). Mile Bjelajac's 1914-1918-online article and Britannica's account of the 1914 campaign give the context.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the defeat on Cer, Austria-Hungary prepared a second invasion with the Fifth and Sixth Armies on the middle and lower Drina, leaving smaller forces on the upper Drina and in Syrmia.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Serbia was meanwhile attacking into Syrmia under Allied pressure and, with Montenegro, into eastern Bosnia. A new invasion would force it back onto the defensive.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Austro-Hungarian plan was to encircle and destroy the main Serbian force in the Jadar valley. The Serbian Second and Third Armies and Colonel Mišić's detachment were deployed along the Drina near Ljubovija to repel the crossings and, if possible, go over to the offensive.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The fighting ran along the Drina and into the mountains of western Serbia: the ridge of Gučevo, Mount Soko and Mačkov Kamen, a summit of the Jagodnja range near Krupanj.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Putnik's Supreme Command commanded the Serbian armies; Potiorek the Austro-Hungarian Fifth and Sixth Armies, whose 15th and 16th Corps took Gučevo. Strengths and losses given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: When the attack came on 8 September, the Serbian First Army was across the Sava in Syrmia and the Užice Army was preparing to enter Bosnia.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 8 September the Fifth and Sixth Armies attacked across the Drina. By 15 September the Sixth Army's 15th and 16th Corps had driven the Serbian Third Army off Gučevo and Mount Soko. The First Army, recalled from Syrmia, reached the Sokolska area on 17 September and eased the pressure on the Third Army's left. The 16th Corps fell back to Mačkov Kamen, which changed hands in seven days of attacks and counterattacks and was taken by the Austro-Hungarians on 24 September. The fronts then settled into trench warfare in October, before a new Austro-Hungarian general attack on 6 November forced the Serbian army to retreat toward Ub and Valjevo.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Serbian Supreme Command broke off the Syrmian offensive and sent the First Army to the Drina, and ordered the Užice Army into Bosnia to threaten the Sixth Army's flank. In November it ordered a retreat to gain time to reinforce its units.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The arrival of the First Army on 17 September stopped the Austro-Hungarian advance from Gučevo; the battle for Mačkov Kamen then exhausted both sides without a breakthrough.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The invasion was held near the river after heavy losses on both sides, and the front settled into a short period of trench warfare. In the museum catalogue's account, the battle ended with the Serbian retreat of November that led into the Kolubara.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Serbian artillery ammunition ran short during the long entrenched fighting, which Bjelajac puts at fifty-five days before the retreat. Sokolović calls Mačkov Kamen one of the bloodiest battles the Serbian army fought in the war; among the dead was Lieutenant-Colonel Dušan Purić, commander of the 4th Regiment. A memorial ossuary designed by Momir Korunović was built on the summit between 1924 and 1936.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Mountain fighting along a river line favours the defender but consumes men and ammunition; a defender with limited industry can win battles and still lose the contest of supply.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources frame the battle differently. Britannica describes a second offensive ending in weeks of deadlock; Tasić a series of smaller clashes and a stalemate in October; the museum catalogue a long battle ending with the Serbian retreat in November. Mačkov Kamen is dated 14–22 September in a source Tasić cites and taken on 24 September in the catalogue. Sokolović's figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Historical Museum of Serbia and Military Museum catalogue gives the narrative. Dmitar Tasić's and Mile Bjelajac's 1914-1918-online articles and Britannica's account of the 1914 campaign give the context and the dates. Miodrag Sokolović's article for the Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments (in Serbian) covers Mačkov Kamen and its ossuary.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In August 1914 two-thirds of the Montenegrin army was placed under the Serbian Supreme Command under a joint plan drawn up by Putnik. Montenegro kept most of its army on the Herzegovina front and at Mount Lovćen, with a smaller force around Pljevlja cooperating with the Serbs.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bjelajac writes that Serbia's allies insisted on offensives across its borders; the move into eastern Bosnia ran in parallel with the crossing into Syrmia.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: With the offensive into Bosnia, the Serbian command wanted to threaten the flank of the Austro-Hungarian Sixth Army fighting on the Drina.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The advance led from the upper Drina into the mountains of eastern Bosnia, toward Srebrenica, Vlasenica and Sarajevo, up to Pale and Mount Romanija on the eastern approaches to Sarajevo.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Serbian Užice Army attacked alongside the Montenegrin Sanjak Army. The sources read here do not name their commanders. Strengths are not given.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Užice Army had been grouped at Užice at the start of the war to support the Montenegrin army, and was positioned on the upper Drina for the offensive.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 13 September the Užice Army and the Sanjak Army crossed the Drina. Tasić dates the capture of Višegrad to 25 September; by the same date, in the museum catalogue's account, the Serbian and Montenegrin troops stood before Pale, Srebrenica and Vlasenica, where they remained into October. Once the front on the middle and lower Drina had stabilised, the Austro-Hungarians reinforced and counterattacked. After the battle of Glasinac the Serbian and Montenegrin units were driven back across the Drina, and by 24 October they had left Bosnia.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Serbian Supreme Command used the Užice Army, together with Montenegrin forces, as an offensive flank guard, threatening the Sixth Army rather than reinforcing the main front on the Drina.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Austro-Hungarian counteroffensive in October, which followed the stabilisation of the main front, ended the advance; Glasinac was the decisive engagement.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Serbian and Montenegrin forces withdrew across the Drina. Tasić notes that the offensive forced a redeployment of Habsburg troops before the counteroffensive.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Austria-Hungary could turn to a third invasion of Serbia in November. The offensive also showed the strains in Serbian–Montenegrin cooperation that Raspopović describes, with Montenegro keeping most of its army for its own fronts.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A diversion against an enemy's flank can draw off troops while the main front holds, but it lasts only until the enemy can spare forces to deal with it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources read here are brief: they give the outline and dates but not the commanders, strengths or the course of the battle of Glasinac. Tasić says the troops took Pale, the museum catalogue that they stood before it. Tasić dates the counteroffensive to mid-October, the museum catalogue to 4 October. Raspopović's article shows that Serbian and Montenegrin aims in Bosnia and Herzegovina were not identical.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Historical Museum of Serbia and Military Museum catalogue and Dmitar Tasić's 1914-1918-online article give the narrative. Mile Bjelajac's and Radoslav Raspopović's articles in the same encyclopedia give the Serbian and Montenegrin context.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Drina fighting, Austria-Hungary launched its third offensive against Serbia on 6 November 1914. Short of artillery ammunition and outnumbered, the Serbian army fell back toward Ub and Valjevo.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: A Serbian defeat would have opened the whole country to occupation. Bjelajac stresses that the army had spent its artillery ammunition in weeks of entrenched fighting and was still waiting for supplies its allies had promised.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Potiorek's Fifth and Sixth Armies, reinforced and resupplied, aimed to break the Serbian line on the Kolubara. The Austro-Hungarian command believed the Serbs held only weak lines on the Kolubara and the Ljig, with their main force in the rear.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Kolubara and its tributary the Ljig run north through western Serbia toward the Sava; to the south rises Mount Suvobor, and Valjevo lies to the west. Belgrade stands where the Sava meets the Danube.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Putnik concentrated all three Serbian armies, the Užice Army and the Obrenovac Detachment on the Kolubara, and organised the defence of Belgrade. Živojin Mišić commanded the First Army. On the other side Potiorek commanded the Fifth and Sixth Armies, with the 13th, 15th and 16th Corps. Strengths and prisoner figures given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 16 November the Fifth Army, supported by the 13th Corps, reached the Kolubara and attacked, but for two days could not break through.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 20 November the Sixth Army struck the Serbian First Army and drove it back across the Ljig to Mount Suvobor. To shorten an over-extended front, the Serbian Supreme Command withdrew to new positions and gave up Belgrade, moving its defenders to Mount Kosmaj; Britannica dates the evacuation to 30 November, and Hall the Austro-Hungarian occupation to 2 December. While the Austro-Hungarian armies regrouped, the Fifth taking Belgrade and the Sixth replacing it in the line, all three Serbian armies attacked on the morning of 3 December. Mišić's First Army took the enemy by surprise; its 1st Danube Division broke through on Suvobor and took Valjevo on 8 December. The 16th Corps' retreat exposed the Austro-Hungarian right and the 15th and 13th Corps fell back in turn. Potiorek ordered the Sixth Army back across the Sava; on 11 December the Serbs attacked the Fifth Army before Belgrade, and on 15 December they entered the city.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Supreme Command chose to shorten the front and abandon Belgrade rather than hold everywhere, then struck while the Austro-Hungarian armies were regrouping.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The First Army's surprise attack from Suvobor on 3 December, and the breakthrough of the 1st Danube Division, unhinged the Austro-Hungarian right and forced the chain retreat of the other corps.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The invading armies were driven out of Serbia for the third time in 1914 and many Austro-Hungarian soldiers were taken prisoner. Britannica notes that mud and exhaustion kept the Serbs from turning the retreat into a rout.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory gave Serbia a long respite from invasion, but its army was exhausted. In the first months of 1915 an epidemic, typhus in Bjelajac's account and typhoid fever in Tasić's, killed many soldiers, wounded men, civilians and Austro-Hungarian prisoners. On 7 December 1914, at Niš, Prime Minister Nikola Pašić first set out a war aim beyond defence: a state uniting the South Slavs.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A defender who trades ground, even the capital, for a shorter front and time to resupply can catch an over-extended attacker in the act of regrouping.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The museum catalogue calls the battle a rare example of a heavy counteroffensive under extreme conditions without reinforcements, a judgment typical of the national narrative. The dates of Belgrade's loss differ (30 November in Britannica, 2 December in Hall), and accounts differ on whether the 1914 invasions numbered two or three. The sources read here do not describe how the Serbian army was resupplied before the counteroffensive.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Historical Museum of Serbia and Military Museum catalogue gives the detailed narrative. Mile Bjelajac's, Dmitar Tasić's and Richard C. Hall's 1914-1918-online articles and Britannica's account of the 1914 campaign and its biography of Putnik give the context, dates and consequences.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After ten months of relative quiet, the Central Powers prepared a new invasion of Serbia in the autumn of 1915. Belgrade, the capital, stood on the frontier where the Sava meets the Danube.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The invasion's main targets were Belgrade and the Morava valley, through which the Central Powers meant to link up with Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire and cut the supply route from Salonika.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Kövess's Austro-Hungarian Third Army aimed at the capital, crossing the Sava and the Danube at Belgrade; Gallwitz's German Eleventh Army crossed farther east toward the Morava valley.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Belgrade's fortress and lower town face the confluence of the Sava and the Danube, with the island of Ciganlija on the Sava upstream. The rivers were the defenders' moat, but the north banks gave the attackers room for heavy batteries.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Serbian defenders included Major Dragutin Gavrilović's men near the railway embankment on the Danube. Russian marine engineers, gunners and mine and torpedo batteries, with British and French guns and men, had come to strengthen the river defences, and a French aviation mission had arrived. Mackensen commanded the Central Powers' offensive. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kövess's batteries opened on Belgrade on 19 September, but at first Serbian artillery and the guns of British sailors prevented a crossing. Heavy guns brought from Poland began a full bombardment on 3 October.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The offensive across the rivers opened on 6 or 7 October. Under heavy fire the Sava and the Danube were crossed, the Danube at Belgrade itself. Artillery made the city untenable, and the Serbs began to evacuate it on 8 October; fighting went on along the quays and in the lower town, where Gavrilović's men held off attacks from both rivers until he ordered them to counterattack. By evening the citadel and the royal palace had fallen, and street fighting continued until Kövess held the whole city on the morning of 9 October.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Serbian command defended the river line at Belgrade but evacuated the city once the crossings succeeded, keeping its army in the field for the campaign to the south.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The arrival of heavy artillery, against which the Serbs had no guns of comparable calibre, made the crossings possible and the city untenable.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Belgrade fell on 9 October 1915. Gavrilović was severely wounded, and many of the defenders were killed and buried along the fortress walls.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: With Belgrade lost, the Serbian army fell back into the interior as Bulgaria joined the attack from the east. After the war the defenders' remains were gathered in an ossuary beside the Jakšić Tower in the fortress, marked by a cross of cannon barrels, and a memorial built in 1931 at the New Cemetery holds the remains of Belgrade's defenders and liberators.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A river line can delay a better-equipped attacker, but once heavy artillery can reach the far bank, a capital on the frontier cannot be held for long.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The opening date is given as 6 October (Bjelajac, Hall) or 7 October (Britannica's chronology and the contemporary Nelson's History). Britannica's chronology says the Germans captured Belgrade; Nelson's History credits Kövess's Austro-Hungarians. Nelson's History is a wartime British account. Gavrilović's famous address to his men does not appear in the sources read here and is not quoted.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Mile Bjelajac's and Richard C. Hall's 1914-1918-online articles give the context and Allied help. The contemporary Nelson's History of the War, read in the Belgrade University Library's digital library, gives the course of the crossings. The Belgrade Fortress and the Serbian Ministry of Defence describe the defenders and their memorials, and Britannica's chronology gives the date of the fall.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the defeats of 1914, the Central Powers wanted to finish with Serbia, for prestige and to secure rail communications with the Ottoman Empire. In September 1915 Bulgaria joined them in return for Serbian territory.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Serbia proposed to strike Bulgaria before it finished mobilising, but its western allies opposed this. Britain and France sent troops to Salonika, but the Greek prime minister who invited them fell from power the day they arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Mackensen's plan was to attack from the north along the Morava valley while Bulgarian armies struck from the east, to link up with Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire and cut Serbia off from Salonika.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The northern armies crossed the Danube and the Sava, then advanced up the Morava valley; the Bulgarians attacked eastern Serbia and the Vardar valley in Macedonia. The Serbian army was pushed back toward the plain of Kosovo.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Mackensen commanded the Austro-Hungarian Third Army, the German Eleventh Army and two Bulgarian armies, with Sarkotić's troops from Bosnia. Putnik's Supreme Command faced them with the First, Second and Third Armies, supported by the Montenegrin army. Tasić puts the Serbs at half the attackers' strength; detailed figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: In the fighting that followed, the First and Third Armies met the attack from the north and the Second Army the Bulgarian First Army in the east.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Austro-German offensive crossed the rivers on 6 or 7 October and took Belgrade on 9 October. Bulgaria attacked eastern Serbia on 11 October and Macedonia on 14 October. In two weeks the northern armies advanced only about thirty kilometres against the First and Third Armies, and the Second Army held the Bulgarian First Army. Reinforced by the German Alpine Corps, the attack pushed forward again at the end of October. The Bulgarian Second Army took Skopje on 22 October, cutting the road to Salonika, and turned toward Kosovo. Niš fell on 6 November. The Serbian army, followed by refugees, withdrew into Kosovo, escaping several attempts to encircle it; Hall writes that it tried to make a stand there but could not hold. On 25 November the Supreme Command ordered a retreat through Montenegro and Albania.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: On 25 November the Supreme Command judged the army unfit for a counteroffensive but capitulation worse, and chose to take the army out of the country to fight on with the Allies.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Bulgarian capture of Skopje on 22 October cut the Serbian army off from the Allies in Salonika and decided the campaign.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Serbia was overrun by the end of November. The Allied force that advanced up the Vardar could not reach the Serbs and fell back into Greece in December.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Central Powers opened the Danube route and the railway to Constantinople. Serbia was divided into an Austro-Hungarian military government and a Bulgarian zone, where the Bulgarian authorities treated the population as Bulgarian and suppressed Serbian schools, names and the Cyrillic alphabet. The Montenegrin army covered the Serbian withdrawal, at heavy cost to itself.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An army attacked from two sides with no reachable ally can still save itself by retreating, if it moves before it is encircled.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Bulgaria's entry is dated 11 October (Britannica), 12 October (Bjelajac) or 14 October (Tasić, and Britannica's chronology for the declaration of war). Bjelajac argues that the Allies arrived too slowly and did not engage on a larger scale. Hall's stand on the old Kosovo battlefield is described only briefly in the sources read here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Mile Bjelajac's 1914-1918-online article gives the most detailed account; Dmitar Tasić's, Richard C. Hall's and Radoslav Raspopović's articles in the same encyclopedia, Britannica's account of the Salonika expedition, its 1915 chronology and its biography of Mackensen give the setting and dates.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By late November 1915 the Serbian army had been driven into Kosovo, cut off from the Allies at Salonika by the Bulgarian advance.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The choice was between capitulation and leaving the country to continue the war beside the Allies. The government, the king and the army all went.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The aim was to reach the Adriatic coast and be carried by Allied ships to safety, keeping the army and the state in being.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The routes led west across the high mountains of Montenegro and Albania to Scutari (Shkodër) and the coast, in winter snow.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Supreme Command, the government of Nikola Pašić, the king and the army moved together with refugees and Austro-Hungarian prisoners. Putnik, ill, was carried in a sedan chair. Numbers given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 25 November the Supreme Command issued the order to retreat through Montenegro and Albania; the Montenegrin army covered the withdrawal.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The columns crossed the Albanian mountains in snow, poorly clothed, without food or medical supplies, and sometimes through hostile villages. Hunger, cold, disease and attacks killed thousands of soldiers, and civilians and prisoners suffered the same. The Serbian Supreme Command took over Scutari, and Pašić reached Cetinje on 22 December to discuss the Montenegrin army's future. A French-led mission under General Piarron de Mondésir organised the rescue from 12 December, and French and Italian ships carried the survivors from the Albanian coast to Corfu, Bizerte and Italy.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Supreme Command chose retreat over surrender, accepting enormous losses to save the army as a fighting force.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Allied evacuation from the Albanian coast, coordinated by an inter-Allied commission in Rome, turned the retreat from a collapse into a recovery.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The army survived. Many of its records were destroyed or only partly saved, so the fate of thousands who did not reach the coast could not be established.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Greek island of Corfu was occupied to receive the army. There the troops recovered and were reorganised, and the Serbian state continued to function until the liberation. In 1916 the rebuilt army sailed from Corfu to the Salonika front. Annual commemorations are held at the mausoleum on the island of Vido and at sea at the place called the Blue Tomb.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An army can be preserved by leaving its country when the alternative is surrender, but only at a terrible cost in lives and with allies able to receive it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The retreat, called the Albanian Golgotha in Serbian memory, is commemorated by the Serbian state; the sources read here do not agree on the numbers lost or rescued, and Bjelajac notes that records were destroyed. Albanian attacks on the columns appear in the Serbian-perspective sources; the Albanian perspective is not represented in the sources read. One British field hospital led by Mabel St Clair Stobart reached the coast without losses.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Mile Bjelajac's 1914-1918-online article gives the most detailed account; Dmitar Tasić's, Richard C. Hall's and Radoslav Raspopović's articles in the same encyclopedia, Britannica's account of the Salonika expedition and its biography of Putnik, and the Serbian Ministry of Defence's report on the Vido commemoration add context and memory.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Montenegro entered the war beside Serbia in 1914, and two-thirds of its army was placed under the Serbian Supreme Command.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: By late 1915 King Nicholas's government was exploring a separate peace with Austria-Hungary, while the Montenegrin army covered the Serbian withdrawal. Raspopović describes it as the Serbian army's strategic protector during the retreat.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The task was to prevent Austro-Hungarian troops from cutting off the Serbian retreat to the Adriatic.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought in Montenegro on the line of the Serbian retreat; the sources read here do not describe the ground at Mojkovac.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: General Janko Vukotić, chief of the Montenegrin Supreme Command headquarters, commanded the Montenegrin troops. The Austro-Hungarian commanders and the strengths of both sides are not given in the sources read here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Montenegrin army had helped the Serbian army withdraw to Kosovo and Metohija and then covered part of it as it crossed Montenegro toward Scutari.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 6 and 7 January 1916 Vukotić's troops dealt the Austro-Hungarians a heavy blow at Mojkovac. Meanwhile Austro-Hungarian forces from the Bay of Kotor attacked Mount Lovćen; Montenegro lost its positions there on 8 and 9 January, and Cetinje was taken after Lovćen fell on 11 January.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Montenegrin command stood and fought on the line of the Serbian retreat rather than withdrawing with the Serbs.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The stand at Mojkovac kept the Austro-Hungarians from cutting off the Serbian retreat; but the breakthrough at Lovćen, where heavy artillery fire from warships was crucial, decided Montenegro's fate.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Serbian retreat was not cut off. Montenegro itself was overrun.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: King Nicholas left the country and made a separate peace, going into exile in Italy. On 18 January Vukotić ordered the last forces to Scutari, leaving each soldier free to go home; on 21 January the government decided to dismiss the army, and the terms of surrender of arms were signed on 25 January. Tasić dates the surrender to 16 January. Thousands of Montenegrin soldiers and civilians were interned in Austria-Hungary. Raspopović argues that the failure to withdraw the army with the Serbs sealed the Montenegrin state's fate.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A rearguard can save an ally's army while its own country is lost; a small army's success depends on decisions made elsewhere.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources read here give only the outline of the battle: not the course of the fighting, the Austro-Hungarian commanders or the strengths. Whether the surrender was a capitulation is disputed, since those who signed lacked authority, and Montenegrin and Serbian accounts differ over the advice a Serbian delegate gave King Nicholas on 1 January.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Dmitar Tasić's and Radoslav Raspopović's 1914-1918-online articles give the battle and its political setting; Britannica's biography of Nicholas I and its 1916 chronology give the outcome.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After recovering on Corfu, the Serbian army was shipped to Salonika in 1916 and given the central part of the Allied front in Macedonia, which by then ran from the Albanian coast to the Aegean.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: In the summer of 1916 Romania was about to join the Entente. The Entente prepared an offensive in Macedonia to divert the Central Powers, and Germany lifted its ban on a Bulgarian advance into Greece so that Bulgaria could strike first.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Bulgarian offensive aimed to pre-empt the Allied attack; the Serbian aim, once it was stopped, was to drive the Bulgarians off the mountain heights and open the way back toward Serbian territory around Bitola.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Kajmakčalan lies in the Nidže range, on today's border between Greece and North Macedonia; its peak, Sveti Ilija, rises to about 2,520 metres and dominates the heights around it.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Serbian First Army attacked the summit; the memorial there is dedicated to its Drina Division. The Bulgarian army held the heights. Maurice Sarrail commanded the Allied armies at Salonika. Commanders' names below army level and strengths are not given in the sources read here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 17 August 1916 the Bulgarians attacked south of Monastir into the Florina region of Greek Macedonia, catching the Allied command and the Serbian forces by surprise while they were on the march.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Serbian troops halted the Bulgarian offensive, winning the battle of Gorničevo near Kela, and went over to the attack. From 12 September the First Army fought for the summit of Kajmakčalan, which it took on 30 September after heavy losses; Bulgarian forces were pushed back to the next mountain chain.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Allied command turned the defence against the Bulgarian offensive into a counteroffensive, giving the Serbian army the task of taking the dominant peaks.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of the summit gave the Serbian army the dominant heights and opened the way for the advance toward Bitola.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Bulgarian offensive in the centre was stopped and turned back, and Kajmakčalan was taken.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The volunteer detachment that included many former irregulars lost so heavily on Kajmakčalan that its survivors were dispersed among regular units. The Serbian Ministry of Defence presents Gorničevo, Kajmakčalan and Bitola together as the recovery of the Serbian army after the retreat through Albania. A memorial chapel and ossuary stand on the summit in memory of the Drina Division.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An army rebuilt in exile could regain its fighting capacity within months; mountain summits that dominate a front repay their high cost.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Serbian commemorations describe the victory as militarily inexplicable without the soldiers' will to return home, a national framing. The sources read here do not name the First Army's commander or give the course of the counterattacks on the summit; Tasić groups Gorničevo, Kajmakčalan and the Crna valley as one series of battles from 17 August to 20 November.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Dmitar Tasić's, Mile Bjelajac's and Richard C. Hall's 1914-1918-online articles and Britannica's account of the Salonika expedition give the narrative and context. Two Serbian Ministry of Defence pages give the dates, the units and the memorial.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In August 1916 the Bulgarians invaded the Florina region; the Allies stopped them and, with the Serbian capture of Kajmakčalan at the end of September, went over to a counteroffensive.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Romania had entered the war on 27 August. The Allied offensive in Macedonia was meant to divert the Central Powers from it.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The objective was Monastir (Bitola), the main town of the region, from which the Bulgarians had launched their August offensive.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The advance led north from Florina and the mountains toward Bitola, through the valley of the Crna river (Crna reka).

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Maurice Sarrail commanded the Allied armies at Salonika, which included French, Serbian, British, Italian and Russian troops. The Central Powers' line here was held mainly by Bulgarian forces, with the German Eleventh Army under German command. Strengths are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: After Kajmakčalan the Serbian army held the dominant peaks, and the Bulgarians had been pushed back to a second mountain line.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Through the autumn the Allies drove the Bulgarians north. The sources read here describe the fighting in the Crna valley only in outline. In November the Allies took Monastir, and Tasić writes that the Central Powers were pushed some forty kilometres north by 20 November.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Allied command used the success on Kajmakčalan to continue the advance rather than stop on the heights, accepting a long autumn campaign in the mountains.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The fall of Monastir ended the advance with a symbolic gain: in Bjelajac's words, the first Serbian ground liberated.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Monastir was taken; the National Army Museum judges the gains limited.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: More ambitious Allied operations from March to May 1917 failed, and the front was quiet for nearly two years. Britannica notes that it tied down a large Allied army without seriously troubling the Central Powers. The Serbian Ministry of Defence counts Bitola, with Gorničevo and Kajmakčalan, as the recovery of the Serbian army.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A coalition offensive in mountains can win ground and symbols but stall short of decisive results when it cannot exploit its successes.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources read here disagree on the offensive's span (12 September to 11 November in the National Army Museum's timeline; 17 August to 20 November in Tasić, including the Bulgarian offensive) and do not give the exact day Monastir fell. They describe the Crna bend fighting only briefly. Serbian sources stress the liberation of Bitola; British and general accounts stress the limited gains.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Dmitar Tasić's, Mile Bjelajac's and Richard C. Hall's 1914-1918-online articles and Britannica's account of the Salonika expedition give the narrative. The National Army Museum's timeline and the Serbian Ministry of Defence's report give the dates and assessments.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the 1915 defeat, Serbia was divided between an Austro-Hungarian military government and a Bulgarian zone in the south and east, with a German zone along the railways. Occupation brought internment, forced labour and requisitions.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Bulgaria treated the territory it occupied as already annexed and its people as Bulgarian: it banned the Serbian Cyrillic alphabet, Serbian names and customs, introduced Bulgarian schools and priests, and interned teachers and priests. Bulgarian attempts in the winter of 1916–1917 to conscript Serbian young men set off the revolt.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Serbian Supreme Command wanted a mass uprising to be prepared for the moment of an Allied breakthrough in Macedonia; in September 1916 it flew Kosta Pećanac into Toplica to organise it. Local leaders insisted on immediate action.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Toplica lies in southern Serbia around Prokuplje and Kuršumlija; its woods gave armed peasants places to gather. The revolt also spread into the southern part of the Austro-Hungarian zone.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The insurgents were led by Pećanac, Kosta Vojinović and other chetnik leaders, with former Montenegrin officers among them. Colonel Alexander Protogerov, head of the Bulgarian military authorities in southern Serbia and a leader of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization, directed the suppression; Austro-Hungarian battalions and Albanian irregular units also took part. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: In Kuršumlija, after the Bulgarians formed an auxiliary gendarmerie of Albanian mercenaries, local people fled into the woods and formed armed companies.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The uprising broke out at the end of February 1917, its most intense phase running from 21 February to 25 March. Near Kuršumlija, on the night of 25–26 February, armed peasants attacked a Bulgarian patrol plundering the village of Mačkovac and drove it back. Vojinović took Kuršumlija, and Pećanac, at his request, defeated a Bulgarian company at Pločnik. The insurgents liberated several small towns and wide rural areas. Bulgarian and Austro-Hungarian forces then counterattacked; Bojović dates their re-entry into Kuršumlija to 16 March, after which they killed, hanged, raped and burned villages without distinction of age or sex.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The insurgent leaders rose before the Allied breakthrough they had been sent to wait for. The occupying powers answered with overwhelming force and reprisals against the population.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The arrival of Bulgarian and Austro-Hungarian reinforcements and the insurgents' lack of weapons and ammunition decided the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The uprising was crushed by late March 1917 with what Ristović calls huge civilian casualties.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The suppression was marked by brutality against civilians, and the deportation of civilians to internment camps increased after the uprising. Pećanac and other leaders escaped and continued a guerrilla campaign that helped the Allied offensive in September 1918.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A rising behind enemy lines can draw off troops, but if it comes too early and without arms it exposes the population to reprisal.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The death toll is reported differently by different sources and is not repeated here. Ristović says the uprising was crushed after two months, Tasić and Bojović by the second half of March. Bojović notes that Serbian historiography long gave the uprising little attention; her article draws on testimonies of survivors and their descendants. Pećanac's later collaboration with the occupiers in the Second World War complicates his memory. The Bulgarian perspective is not represented in the sources read here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Dmitar Tasić's 1914-1918-online article and his biography of Pećanac give the course of the uprising, and Milan Ristović's article on occupation gives its setting and toll. Stojanka Bojović's article for the Historical Archives of Niš records the events in Kuršumlija.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Monastir the Macedonian front stood largely still for nearly two years. Sarrail was replaced at the end of 1917 by Guillaumat, and in the summer of 1918 by Louis Franchet d'Espèrey. In June a Greek and French attack on the fortified ridge of Skra di Legen showed how far Bulgarian morale had fallen.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: With the Germans retreating on the Western Front, a breakthrough in Macedonia offered the Entente a back door into Austria-Hungary and toward Constantinople, and a way to divert Central Powers resources. Bulgaria's soldiers lacked food and clothing, and its relations with its allies were strained.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The aim was to break the Bulgarian line at Dobro Pole, reach the flatter ground behind it and the Vardar valley, and go on to Skopje and into Serbia. Hall writes that the idea came from a Serbian staff officer as early as 1916.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Dobro Pole is a mountain ridge in the centre of the Macedonian front, on today's border between Greece and North Macedonia. The Bulgarians had fortified it since 1916 with two main trench lines, barbed wire and artillery behind; beyond it lay the more open ground that gave it its name.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Franchet d'Espèrey attacked with six Serbian and two French divisions against a seven-mile front held by a single Bulgarian division; Bjelajac describes the Serbian Second Army, reinforced by two French divisions in the first line, making the main breach. Živojin Mišić was chief of the Serbian High Command. By the summer the Entente had a clear superiority in men and equipment. Detailed figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Entente had built up its forces in front of Dobro Pole through the summer. A French report of 15 September described the Bulgarian army and people as overcome by a desire for peace.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: After a night bombardment, the assault opened on the morning of 15 September (Hall dates the start to the 14th), and by nightfall on the 16th a penetration of five miles had been made. The next day the Serbs advanced twenty miles while French and Greek forces widened the breach. A British and Greek attack at Lake Doiran from 18 September held Bulgarian troops in place, although the Bulgarians repulsed it. By 19 September Serbian cavalry had reached Kavadarci, and two days later the Bulgarian front west of the Vardar had collapsed. Bulgarian units on either side withdrew to avoid being cut off, and disorderly groups of soldiers headed home.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Franchet d'Espèrey concentrated the attack on a narrow mountain sector where the Serbian army had long wanted to strike, and used the Doiran attack to keep Bulgarian reserves from the breach.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The breach at Dobro Pole could not be sealed: the Bulgarian army, its morale already broken, could not regroup, and the Serbian armies pursued it and crushed every attempt by its reserves.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: On 25 September the Bulgarian government decided to seek an armistice. On 29 September, as French cavalry took Skopje, Bulgaria signed an armistice at Salonika, the first of the Central Powers to leave the war. The National Army Museum calls the offensive the decisive attack on the Salonika front.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Mutinous soldiers proclaimed a republic at Radomir on 27 September; German troops, cadets and IMRO forces turned them back near Pernik on 30 September, and Tsar Ferdinand abdicated on 3 October. The way into Serbia and toward the Danube lay open; Britannica credits Franchet d'Espèrey with opening the road to Vienna for the Allies.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A front held by a demoralised and poorly supplied army can collapse at a single well-prepared breach, and the collapse can spread far beyond the battlefield.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Hall dates the assault to 14 September, Britannica to the 15th; the armistice was signed on 29 September (Hall, Britannica) and is sometimes dated 30 September (Tasić). Hall stresses that hunger, poor equipment and strained alliances were as effective as Serbian infantry and French artillery; Serbian commemorations present the breakthrough above all as a Serbian victory. The sources read here do not name the Serbian army commanders at Dobro Pole.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Richard C. Hall's 1914-1918-online articles on the war in the Balkans and on Bulgaria give the fullest account, with Mile Bjelajac's and Dmitar Tasić's articles in the same encyclopedia. Britannica's account of the Balkan front in 1918 and its biography of Franchet d'Espèrey give the sequence and assessment; the National Army Museum's timeline and the Serbian Ministry of Defence add dates and framing.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Serbia had been occupied for three years, divided between Austria-Hungary and Bulgaria. The breakthrough at Dobro Pole opened the way north from Macedonia.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: With Bulgaria out of the war, the German High Command hoped to build a new Balkan front to save Austria-Hungary. The Serbian advance was also a political event: news of it gave momentum to the movement for South Slav unification.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Serbian armies and their allies aimed to liberate Serbia before the Central Powers could form a new front, then cross the Drina, Sava and Danube into Austria-Hungary.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The advance followed the Vardar valley north through Macedonia to Skopje, then the Morava valley through Niš to Belgrade on the Danube.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Serbian First Army led the pursuit with French cavalry beside it; Živojin Mišić was chief of the Serbian High Command, and Franchet d'Espèrey commanded the Allied armies. German and Austro-Hungarian units opposed the advance, and the sources read here do not give their strength.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: By late September Serbian troops were already north of the broken front, taking Veles and Štip on 26 September, while French cavalry took Skopje on 29 September.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Serbian First Army and French cavalry pushed rapidly into the Morava valley. Niš was taken on 10 October (Hall) or 12 October (Tasić), cutting the land route to the Ottoman Empire. Insurgents in occupied Serbia joined in: Kosta Pećanac began full-scale guerrilla warfare and captured many prisoners. German and Austro-Hungarian troops withdrew from Serbia and Montenegro by the end of October, and Serbian troops reached Belgrade on 31 October; all of pre-war Serbia was free by 1 November. Franchet d'Espèrey then ordered small detachments across the Drina, Sava and Danube, and Serbian troops moved into southern Hungary.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: From 3 November Franchet d'Espèrey's instructions, in line with Mišić's orders to his army commanders, directed the Serbian army to support the South Slav movements in Bosnia, Croatia and Vojvodina; Franchet d'Espèrey also wanted troops to keep order along the railways and in the main cities.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The capture of Niš destroyed German hopes of forming a new Balkan front and cut communications with the Ottoman Empire.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Serbia was liberated by 1 November 1918. Hungary signed an armistice in Belgrade on 13 November, the last of the war.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: On 1 December 1918 the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was proclaimed in Belgrade. The museum catalogue notes that Serbia suffered the greatest demographic loss of any belligerent in proportion to its population; Tasić writes that the exact civilian toll, from hunger, occupation and the influenza pandemic, remains unknown.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A pursuit that keeps moving can prevent a defeated enemy from forming a new front; local insurgents can multiply its effect.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The dates for Niš (10 or 12 October) and Belgrade (31 October or 1 November) differ between the sources. Bjelajac stresses that Franchet d'Espèrey's orders had political as well as military aims. The museum catalogue and Bjelajac present the advance as the culmination of Serbia's war; Britannica emphasises Franchet d'Espèrey's thrust to the Danube.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Mile Bjelajac's, Dmitar Tasić's and Richard C. Hall's 1914-1918-online articles, with Tasić's biography of Pećanac, give the course of the liberation. Britannica's account of the Balkan front and its biography of Franchet d'Espèrey give the Allied side, and the Historical Museum of Serbia and Military Museum catalogue the cost of the war.

phases.title: Through Macedonia
phases.description: Serbian troops take Veles and Štip; French cavalry takes Skopje.

phases.title: Up the Morava
phases.description: The First Army and French cavalry advance; Niš falls on 10 or 12 October.

phases.title: Belgrade
phases.description: Serbian troops reach Belgrade; all of pre-war Serbia is free.

phases.title: Across the rivers
phases.description: Detachments cross into Austria-Hungary; Hungary signs an armistice in Belgrade on 13 November.

perspectives.name: Živojin Mišić
perspectives.objective: Liberate Serbia before a new front could form, and support South Slav unification.
perspectives.known: Bulgaria had left the war and the Central Powers had few troops in the Balkans.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether German reinforcements would stop the advance in the Morava valley.
perspectives.constraints: Long marches from Macedonia and stretched supply lines.
perspectives.forces: The Serbian armies with French cavalry, helped by insurgents.
perspectives.terrain: The Vardar and Morava valleys to the Danube.
perspectives.logistics: Supply over a rapidly lengthening route from Salonika.
perspectives.decision: He kept up the pursuit and directed army commanders to support the South Slav movements.
perspectives.outcome: Serbia was liberated by 1 November.

perspectives.name: German and Austro-Hungarian command
perspectives.objective: Form a new Balkan front after Bulgaria's collapse.
perspectives.known: The Serbian and French advance was moving fast up the Morava.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether reinforcements could arrive in time.
perspectives.constraints: Too few troops to plug all the gaps.
perspectives.forces: German and Austro-Hungarian units in Serbia, with divisions promised from elsewhere.
perspectives.terrain: The Morava valley and Niš.
perspectives.logistics: Lines through an occupied, rebellious country.
perspectives.decision: They tried to hold the Morava valley, then withdrew.
perspectives.outcome: They left Serbia and Montenegro by the end of October.
